prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT treat this second episode of pneumococcal meningitis in isolation without investigating for an anatomical or immunological predisposing cause — failure to do so guarantees further recurrence and potentially fatal episodes.
Do NOT delay empiric IV antibiotics while awaiting imaging or LP when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.

Do not delay lumbar puncture or antibiotics to obtain a CT head: cranial imaging is not routine before lumbar puncture (WHO 2025 section A.4; NICE NG240 1.4.6) and no imaging-first criterion is present.

Do NOT attribute the chronic unilateral watery rhinorrhea to allergic rhinitis without beta-2-transferrin testing — the reservoir sign and unilateral clear rhinorrhea in the context of recurrent meningitis demand CSF-leak confirmation.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for bacterial meningitis.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.
Draw two sets of blood cultures BEFORE the first antibiotic dose.

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 14, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilledema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.
Send full CSF panel at LP: cell count/differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, multiplex PCR, and CSF lactate.

Confirm the CSF leak with beta-2 transferrin on the left nasal secretion, collected while the rhinorrhea is active; it is a send-out assay reported in about 3 days, so antibiotics, dexamethasone and the skull-base imaging proceed without waiting for it.

Investigate the predisposing cause of recurrence: CT of the anterior skull base with thin-section bone windows and contrast MRI to characterize the defect; send quantitative immunoglobulins and complement (C3, C4, CH50) to exclude humoral or complement deficiency.
Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: continue ceftriaxone, or switch to benzylpenicillin (penicillin MIC 0.06 mg/L, susceptible), for 14 days.
Arrange ENT and neurosurgical consultations for elective endoscopic skull-base repair of the cribriform plate defect after acute infection is controlled, to prevent further recurrence.
Offer pneumococcal conjugate vaccination after recovery (PCV20 or PCV21, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23): a CSF leak is an indication.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded by CSF pathogen identification.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

key_clinical_evidence: Recurrent bacterial meningitis is not a random event — it ALWAYS requires investigation for an anatomical defect (CSF fistula) or an immune defect (antibody deficiency, complement deficiency, asplenia); treating each episode in isolation is a serious omission.

Beta-2-transferrin assay on nasal secretions is the gold-standard diagnostic test for CSF rhinorrhea, with sensitivity >90% and near-perfect specificity; positive result confirms the nasal discharge is CSF.

The 'reservoir sign' (increased rhinorrhea on leaning forward) and unilateral constant clear watery discharge, especially in the context of prior head trauma, are cardinal features of CSF rhinorrhea that must not be attributed to allergic rhinitis without confirmatory testing.

Skull-base CT with high-resolution bone-algorithm coronal reconstructions is first-line imaging to localise the bony defect and guide surgical planning; MRI with gadolinium provides complementary soft tissue characterisation and detects meningoencephalocele.
Normal immunoglobulins and CH50 effectively exclude CVID and terminal complement deficiency as the predisposing cause, making the anatomical defect the unifying diagnosis in this case.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).
Definitive prevention of further recurrence requires surgical repair of the cribriform plate defect (typically endoscopic endonasal approach) combined with pneumococcal vaccination.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

No WHO 2025 section A.4 imaging-first criterion is present (GCS 14, no focal signs, cranial nerve deficit, papilledema, seizure or severe immunocompromise), so lumbar puncture proceeds without prior imaging; the skull-base CT is ordered to find the defect, not to clear the lumbar puncture.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A second episode of bacterial meningitis within 14 months with the same organism is the sentinel event that should trigger immediate investigation for anatomical or immune predisposition — each episode treated in isolation is a diagnostic failure.

metadata.condition_name: Recurrent acute bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae with CSF rhinorrhea from left cribriform plate defect
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: each isolated episode looks like routine community-acquired pneumococcal meningitis. The critical clue — second episode within 14 months plus a 3-year history of positional clear left-sided rhinorrhea previously attributed to allergic rhinitis — is the pivot that should trigger a structured anatomical/immunological workup. The agent must recognise the recurrence pattern, connect the rhinorrhea to a CSF leak, order beta-2-transferrin and skull-base imaging, exclude immune causes, and recommend surgical referral — rather than simply treating the acute episode and discharging.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 6 required actions (labs, blood cultures, CSF, skull-base CT, contrast MRI, nasal beta-2 transferrin); 3 embedded red herrings (rhinorrhea misdiagnosed as allergic rhinitis, anchoring on isolated-episode framing, sinusitis as alternative focus); requires synthesis across CSF, CT, MRI and immune labs to diagnose both the acute infection and the underlying anatomical predisposition; normal immune workup means the puzzle has only one unifying answer (structural defect).
metadata.real_seed_note: Clinical pattern seeded from published literature on recurrent bacterial meningitis with CSF leak (ter Horst et al., Clin Infect Dis 2019, PMID 31300817; CC-BY-NC-ND open access) and supporting case reports (PMC5551538, PMID 28819362, CC-BY). No single published case was reproduced verbatim. The case was authored de novo with distinct demographics (28-year-old South Asian male), a left cribriform plate defect post minor head trauma, a 14-month inter-episode interval, and an explicitly normal immune workup, making the anatomical defect the sole demonstrated predisposing cause. The diagnostic puzzle (overlooked CSF rhinorrhea attributed to allergic rhinitis) and the recurrence flag as the key pivot are consistent with epidemiological and case-report data from the cited sources.
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 meningitis audit: complete LP/microbiology/lab pathway, no ECG, and MRI restricted to complications or non-response

patient.history_present_illness:
A 28-year-old South Asian man presents to the emergency department with an 18-hour history of rapidly progressive severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and fever. This is his second episode of bacterial meningitis within 14 months. His first episode occurred 14 months ago at another hospital, where he was admitted with an identical syndrome of fever, headache, and meningismus and was diagnosed with Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis by CSF culture. He was treated with 14 days of IV ceftriaxone, recovered fully, and was discharged with no further workup to identify an underlying predisposing cause. At that time, neither a skull-base CT nor an immunological workup was performed, and no follow-up with an ENT or neurosurgeon was arranged.

For the past three years, the patient has had chronic intermittent clear watery discharge from the left nostril. He had been evaluated by an allergist approximately 18 months ago, was skin-tested and found to have mild sensitisation to house dust mite, and was diagnosed with allergic rhinitis. Antihistamines and an intranasal corticosteroid were prescribed. He describes the nasal discharge as 'like water' and notices it is especially prominent when he bends forward or tilts his head, and when he lies flat. He reports that it is always unilateral, left-sided, and clear — it has never been purulent. He did not connect this symptom to his episode of meningitis 14 months ago. He has a history of a minor motorcycle accident at age 24, which caused a mild head injury; a CT brain at that time was reported as normal, but no dedicated imaging of the skull base was performed.

The current episode began yesterday morning with a diffuse, rapidly worsening headache that he rated 10 out of 10 within hours. He developed neck stiffness that prevented him from touching his chin to his chest. Fever was documented by thermometer at 39.0 degrees Celsius at home. He developed severe photophobia and nausea. He presented to the ED approximately 18 hours after symptom onset. On arrival, he immediately recognised the syndrome as identical to his prior episode. He has not taken any antibiotics in the week prior to presentation. He is otherwise healthy with no chronic medical conditions, no immunosuppressive medications, and no sick contacts.

neurological_exam.additional: Marked nuchal rigidity present — passive neck flexion restricted and painful. Kernig sign positive bilaterally. Brudzinski sign positive. No petechiae, purpura, or skin rash. Nasal examination by ER physician: watery clear discharge noted from the left naris, more prominent with the patient leaning forward (positive reservoir sign). No lymphadenopathy.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin accurate without dysmetria bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, briskly reactive. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact; no nystagmus, no diplopia. Mild bilateral photophobia — patient repeatedly asks for lights to be dimmed. No papilledema on direct fundoscopy. Facial sensation and motor symmetric. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Not formally assessed — patient refuses to stand due to severe headache and photophobia.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but appears markedly ill, restless, and photophobic. Oriented to person and place; disoriented to date. GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6). Difficulty concentrating; unable to perform serial subtraction beyond two steps. Speech fluent without aphasia.
neurological_exam.motor: Strength 5/5 throughout all extremities. No pronator drift. Normal bulk and tone.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patella, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact and symmetric in all extremities. Proprioception intact at bilateral great toes.
